name: Anterior shoulder dislocation (with Bankart/Hill–Sachs)
summary: The humeral head is forced forward out of the glenoid, usually in abduction, external rotation and extension, tearing the anteroinferior labrum (Bankart) and often denting the humeral head (Hill–Sachs).

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation over about 3–6 months; after surgical stabilisation about 6 months before contact sport (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not before about 3 months after non-operative care or about 6 months after stabilisation

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Relocation test (LR+ 6.5) and anterior release test (LR+ 8.3)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs before and after reduction; MRI or MR arthrography for labrum and cuff; CT for bone loss

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 20–29 years; 71.8% of emergency department cases are male

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: About 39% overall in adults; markedly higher at 40 years or under

overview:
Acute anterior shoulder dislocation is the most common type of shoulder dislocation [r1]. The humeral head leaves the glenoid forward and below the coracoid, usually after a fall or a contact force on an abducted, externally rotated and extended arm. In young people the capsulolabral complex is detached from the anteroinferior glenoid rim (a Bankart or Perthes–Bankart lesion) in nearly all first-time dislocations, and the posterolateral humeral head is commonly dented against the glenoid rim (a Hill–Sachs lesion) [r2].

The central clinical problem is recurrence. Across ten studies of adults, recurrent instability followed 39% of first-time traumatic anterior dislocations, and the odds were about 13 times higher at 40 years or under [r3]. Non-operative care is still reasonable: in a 25-year cohort of people aged 12–40 years, 43% never re-dislocated, and in those aged 12–25 years about half had not recurred or had become stable [r4]. Surgical stabilisation lowers recurrence in randomised trials [r5], but a pooled analysis found no significant difference in functional scores, so immediate surgery may not suit everyone [r6].

Acute care is prompt closed reduction with a neurovascular check before and after. Several techniques work [r7]. Immobilisation after reduction did not change the prognosis [r4], and the evidence on external-rotation versus internal-rotation immobilisation is very low certainty [r1]. Rehabilitation, preferably neuromuscular and criteria-based, is the physiotherapist's central role in both pathways [r8].

epidemiology.text: A national sample of United States emergency departments estimated an incidence of 23.9 per 100,000 person-years for all shoulder dislocations; the male rate was 34.9, 2.64 times the female rate [r9]. Men made up 71.8% of cases, and the highest incidence, 47.8 per 100,000, was in the 20–29 year decade; 46.8% of all dislocations occurred between 15 and 29 years of age [r9]. Dislocations most often resulted from a fall (58.8%) and occurred at home (47.7%) or at a sports or recreation site (34.5%); 48.3% occurred during sport or recreation [r9]. Recurrence is common: 39% after a first dislocation in adults [r3], and the risk falls as time from the first dislocation increases [r3].

intrinsic: Age 40 years or under at the first dislocation (odds ratio 13.46 for recurrence) [r3]
A concomitant greater tuberosity fracture lowers the risk of recurrence (odds ratio 0.13) [r3]
A bony Bankart lesion, Hill–Sachs lesion or nerve palsy were also linked with recurrence, but evidence was weak [r3]
extrinsic: Contact and collision sports, especially in-season athletes with a first event [r10]
Falls, the commonest cause of dislocation presenting to emergency departments [r9]
Overhead and combative sports that load the arm in abduction and external rotation
Time since the first dislocation: recurrence is highest early [r3]

mechanism.summary: The classic mechanism is a force that drives an abducted, externally rotated arm further into external rotation and extension, such as an arm tackle, a fall onto the outstretched or abducted arm, or a forced throw. The humeral head levers over the anteroinferior glenoid rim, tears the anterior capsulolabral complex and comes to rest forward of and below the coracoid. The posterolateral head impacts the glenoid rim on the way, producing a Hill–Sachs impaction.
sequence: The arm is abducted to about 90° with the shoulder in external rotation and extension, for example when reaching to tackle, block or break a fall.
A sudden force from a tackle, collision or fall drives the arm further into external rotation and extension.
The humeral head levers forward against the anteroinferior capsule, the anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament and the labrum.
The capsulolabral complex fails and is detached from the anteroinferior glenoid rim and neck (Perthes–Bankart lesion) [r2].
The head slides forward and inferiorly into a subcoracoid position, and the posterolateral head is impacted by the glenoid rim (Hill–Sachs lesion) [r2].
Bleeding fills the joint (haemarthrosis), and the cuff, deltoid and pectoralis major spasm and hold the head out of the socket.
Closed reduction restores alignment, but the labral tear and the humeral head defect remain.

variants.name: Contact or collision (tackle) dislocation
variants.description: A high-energy force on the abducted arm in rugby, football, hockey or martial arts. In intercollegiate contact athletes with an in-season event, only 40% managed non-operatively returned to play without recurrence the next season [r10].

variants.name: Fall onto the arm
variants.description: Falls cause most dislocations presenting to emergency departments (58.8%) [r9]. In people over 40, falls are more often associated with a rotator cuff tear [r11] or nerve injury [r12].

variants.name: Recurrent or low-energy dislocation
variants.description: After a first dislocation, later episodes can occur with minimal force or during sleep or daily tasks as the labrum, capsule and bone defects reduce stability. Management tends to shift toward surgical stabilisation.

variants.name: Subluxation
variants.description: Partial, self-reducing translation of the head with a 'dead arm' or apprehension. It uses the same pathology as a dislocation but may not need emergency reduction.

anatomy.text: The glenohumeral joint is a ball-and-socket joint with a large humeral head articulating with a small, shallow glenoid. The glenoid labrum deepens the socket, and the capsule with its thickened ligaments gives static stability, especially at the end of range. In the abducted, externally rotated position, the anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL) is the key restraint to anterior translation. Dynamic stability comes from the rotator cuff, which compresses the head into the glenoid, from the long head of biceps, and from the scapular muscles that position the glenoid. The axillary nerve passes close to the inferior capsule and around the surgical neck of the humerus, which is why it is at risk.

structures.name: Anteroinferior glenoid labrum
structures.role: Fibrocartilage rim that deepens the socket and anchors the capsule and IGHL; the site of the Bankart lesion

structures.name: Inferior glenohumeral ligament (anterior band)
structures.role: Primary static restraint to anterior translation with the arm abducted and externally rotated

structures.name: Glenohumeral capsule
structures.role: Sleeve of tissue that limits end-range translation and rotation

structures.name: Subscapularis and anterior rotator cuff
structures.role: Dynamic anterior stabiliser; stretched and sometimes torn in dislocation

structures.name: Humeral head and greater tuberosity
structures.role: The posterolateral head is the site of the Hill–Sachs impaction; the greater tuberosity may fracture

structures.name: Axillary nerve
structures.role: Supplies deltoid and teres minor and the skin over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area)

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In a series of 63 patients under 24 years (average age 19.6 years) who had arthroscopy within 10 days of a first traumatic anterior dislocation, all had haemarthrosis, 61 (97%) had complete detachment of the capsuloligamentous complex from the glenoid rim and neck (Perthes–Bankart lesion), and 57 had Hill–Sachs lesions, none of them large [r2]. One patient had an IGHL avulsion from the humeral neck and one had an interstitial capsular tear, six had superior labral (SLAP) lesions, and none had a rotator cuff tear [r2]. In the 53 young patients who chose non-operative treatment, 48 (90%) developed recurrent instability, which suggests a strong association between the Perthes–Bankart lesion and recurrence in this population [r2].

Older patients have a different injury pattern. Rotator cuff tears may occur after dislocation, either in younger athletes or in older people with age-related tendon degeneration, and persistent pain or weakness after dislocation often indicates a concomitant cuff tear [r11]. Nerve injury is also common: in a prospective EMG study of 101 patients with primary dislocation or humeral neck fracture, 45% had electrophysiological evidence of nerve injury, mainly of the axillary, suprascapular, radial and musculocutaneous nerves, and these injuries were commoner in older patients and in those with a haematoma [r12].

structures.name: Anteroinferior labrum and capsule (Bankart lesion)
structures.effect: Detached from the glenoid rim and neck in 97% of the young first-time dislocations treated surgically in one series [r2]; the key lesion behind recurrent instability

structures.name: Inferior glenohumeral ligament
structures.effect: Avulsed from the glenoid or, rarely, from the humeral neck (HAGL); loses its role as the anterior restraint [r2]

structures.name: Posterolateral humeral head (Hill–Sachs lesion)
structures.effect: Impaction defect from contact with the glenoid rim; present in 57 of 63 patients in the series, none of them large [r2]

structures.name: Anteroinferior glenoid rim (bony Bankart)
structures.effect: Fracture of the rim with attached labrum; reported as a risk factor for recurrence but the evidence was weak [r3]

structures.name: Greater tuberosity
structures.effect: May fracture; only 2 of 24 shoulders with a greater tuberosity fracture re-dislocated in a 25-year cohort [r4]

structures.name: Rotator cuff
structures.effect: Tears occur after dislocation, especially in people over 40 years, and should be considered if weakness or pain persists [r11]

structures.name: Axillary nerve
structures.effect: Stretched or contused, causing deltoid weakness and lateral shoulder numbness; most nerve injuries recovered partially or completely in under 4 months, and 8 of 101 had persistent motor loss [r12]

muscles.name: Pectoralis major, deltoid and rotator cuff
muscles.effect: Protective spasm holds the head out of the socket and makes reduction harder without analgesia or sedation

muscles.name: Rotator cuff (especially subscapularis and infraspinatus)
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition and weakness after reduction; dynamic stability and joint position sense are reduced

muscles.name: Deltoid and teres minor
muscles.effect: Weak or paralysed if the axillary nerve is injured, with later atrophy if the nerve does not recover

muscles.name: Scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, trapezius)
muscles.effect: Often show delayed activation and altered scapular control that needs retraining

cellular.description: Haemarthrosis, platelet plug, then neutrophils and macrophages clear debris from the torn capsulolabral tissue and the impacted bone.

Fibroblasts and new capillaries lay down disorganised type III collagen. The capsulolabral avulsion is strongly associated with recurrent instability in young patients [r2], and the torn labrum often does not re-attach firmly to the glenoid rim.
Collagen is slowly replaced by aligned type I fibres along lines of load. Any scar is typically lax compared with the intact capsulolabral complex.
Most axillary and other nerve injuries recovered partially or completely within 4 months, but some leave persistent motor loss [r12].

systems.effect: Axillary nerve injury is a recognised complication [r12], and proprioception and reflex stabilisation are reduced after dislocation, so neuromuscular training is central to rehabilitation [r8]
Haemarthrosis, and in rare cases axillary artery injury, especially in older people or after a delayed or forceful reduction
Apprehension and kinesiophobia (fear of movement) are common and affect return to sport; they were measured as secondary outcomes in a randomised trial of neuromuscular exercise [r8]
Scapular dyskinesis, thoracic stiffness and lower-limb and trunk drive during throwing or contact affect shoulder loading after injury
Synovitis and capsular inflammation settle over weeks; persistent stiffness can follow immobilisation, and a stiff shoulder may later evolve toward frozen shoulder (see frozen shoulder)

grading.system: Patterns of structural injury (descriptive; there is no validated grading)

grades.description: Capsulolabral complex detached from the anteroinferior glenoid rim and neck, present in 97% of young first-time dislocations treated surgically in one series [r2].
grades.prognosis: Strongly associated with recurrent instability: 90% of the young non-operative patients in the same series developed it [r2].

grades.description: Fracture of the anteroinferior glenoid rim with the labrum attached.
grades.prognosis: A reported risk factor for recurrence, though the evidence is weak [r3]. Larger bone loss usually changes the surgical approach.

grades.description: Impaction defect of the posterolateral humeral head. In one series 57 of 63 patients had one, none large [r2].
grades.prognosis: A reported risk factor for recurrence with weak evidence [r3]; larger defects that engage the glenoid rim may favour surgery.

grades.grade: Humeral avulsion of the IGHL (HAGL) or capsular tear
grades.description: The ligament tears off the humeral neck, or the capsule tears in its substance. Uncommon: one of each in the series of 63 [r2].
grades.prognosis: Needs a different surgical technique from a standard Bankart repair.

grades.description: Associated avulsion fracture of the greater tuberosity, often in older patients.
grades.prognosis: Lower risk of recurrence (odds ratio 0.13) [r3]; only 2 of 24 re-dislocated in a 25-year cohort [r4]. Check the cuff and displacement.

timeframes.summary: Pain settles over days to weeks after reduction, but the labral and capsular lesion does not reliably heal, so function and stability depend on rehabilitation. Recurrence is highest early after the first dislocation and decreases with time [r3].

healing.description: Reduction, short sling use for comfort, pain control and early gentle movement in a protected range.
Haemarthrosis resolves, fibroblasts lay down early scar and nerve injuries begin to recover.
Progressive cuff and scapular strengthening and rhythmic stabilisation, with increasing range.
Collagen remodelling with high-load strength, plyometrics and sport-specific training.

milestones.label: Comfortable without sling
milestones.note: Typical; sling is for comfort only

milestones.label: Return to contact or collision sport
milestones.note: Commonly about 6 months after surgical stabilisation (clinical convention)

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based and individual. Commonly not before about 3 months for non-operative care and about 6 months after surgical stabilisation for contact and collision sport (clinical conventions). In-season athletes face a decision between playing on with high recurrence risk and off-season stabilisation [r10].

symptoms: Sudden severe shoulder pain after a fall, tackle or forced arm movement, often with a feeling that the shoulder 'came out'
Inability to move the arm, which is held slightly abducted and supported by the other hand
Numbness or tingling over the outer shoulder or into the arm (nerve involvement)
A history of previous dislocations or recurrent 'giving way' in recurrent instability
Apprehension with the arm in the abducted and externally rotated position after reduction
signs: Squared-off shoulder contour with a prominent acromion and a hollow below it
Anterior fullness from the displaced head, palpable below the coracoid
Arm held in slight abduction and external rotation, with marked loss of passive external rotation
Reduced or absent sensation over the lateral deltoid (regimental badge area) and weak deltoid contraction in axillary nerve injury
Haemarthrosis and bruising developing over days
After reduction: positive apprehension and relocation tests, and generalised laxity in some people

subjective: Mechanism: arm position (abducted, externally rotated, extended), force, fall or contact, and whether the shoulder was reduced and by whom
Number of previous dislocations or subluxations, and ease of recurrence (low-energy or in sleep)
Age, dominant arm, sport, level and position, season timing and goals
Neurological symptoms: numbness, weakness, burning pain or arm heaviness
Hyperlaxity history (other joints), previous surgery, seizures or electrical injury (posterior dislocation)
Psychological readiness, fear of re-injury and expectations about surgery
observation: Acute: squared shoulder, arm position and obvious deformity
Skin integrity, bruising and swelling after reduction
Deltoid and cuff bulk and symmetry in the subacute and chronic phase
Scapular position and dyskinesis during elevation and lowering
palpation: Anterior shoulder and coracoid region tenderness
Greater tuberosity and bicipital groove tenderness (fracture, cuff, biceps)
Posterior joint line and infraspinatus (Hill–Sachs side) tenderness
AC joint and clavicle to exclude associated injury
rangeOfMotion: Acute: do not force external rotation or abduction before imaging and reduction
Subacute: pain-limited elevation and rotation compared with the other side
Assess for generalised hypermobility with the Beighton score, given hyperlaxity as a risk factor [r3]
Measure external rotation in adduction and at 90° abduction in later stages
strength: Isometric deltoid contraction (axillary nerve motor check) before and after reduction
Rotator cuff strength: external rotation, internal rotation and abduction, comparing sides with a hand-held dynamometer
External rotation lag sign and drop-arm sign if over 40 years or if weakness persists, to detect a cuff tear [r11]
Scapular strength and endurance (serratus anterior, lower trapezius)
neuro: Axillary nerve: sensation over the lateral deltoid and deltoid isometric contraction, documented before and after reduction
Full upper limb screen: musculocutaneous, radial, median and ulnar sensory and motor function, and brachial plexus signs
Vascular: radial pulse, capillary refill, temperature and colour of the hand
Repeat the neurological screen at follow-up if any deficit was present
functional: Overhead reach, hand behind back and sleep position tolerance
Closed-chain stability: wall push-up plus and quadruped weight shifts
Sport-specific tasks (throwing, tackling, overhead catch) once strength and range allow

specialTests.name: Apprehension test
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine, arm abducted to 90° and elbow flexed. Gradually externally rotate the shoulder while watching for apprehension.
specialTests.positive: Apprehension or fear that the shoulder will dislocate (not pain alone). A systematic review found it less useful for diagnosis than the relocation test [r13].

specialTests.name: Relocation test
specialTests.procedure: From the apprehension position, apply a posteriorly directed force to the proximal humerus.
specialTests.positive: Apprehension or pain relieved, allowing further external rotation.

specialTests.name: Anterior release (surprise) test
specialTests.procedure: Perform the relocation test, then suddenly release the posterior force.
specialTests.positive: Sudden return of apprehension or pain.

specialTests.name: Sulcus sign
specialTests.procedure: With the arm at the side, apply downward traction on the arm and look for a sulcus below the acromion.
specialTests.positive: A visible sulcus that does not reduce with external rotation. Considered less useful than the relocation test for diagnosing anterior instability [r13].

specialTests.name: Deltoid isometric contraction and regimental badge sensation
specialTests.procedure: Ask the patient to push the arm into abduction against your hand without moving the shoulder, and compare light-touch sensation over the lateral deltoid with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Absent contraction or reduced sensation. Document before and after reduction.

clinicalRules.name: Neurovascular examination before and after reduction
clinicalRules.description: Document the axillary nerve and distal pulses before any reduction attempt and again afterwards. Most nerve injuries recover partially or completely within 4 months [r12].

clinicalRules.name: Radiograph before reduction when fracture is possible
clinicalRules.description: Obtain AP, scapular Y and axillary views to exclude fracture-dislocation and Hill–Sachs or bony Bankart lesions (standard practice). Repeat after reduction to confirm alignment.

outcomeMeasures.name: Western Ontario Shoulder Instability Index (WOSI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Instability-specific quality of life; the primary outcome in a randomised trial of neuromuscular exercise [r8] and used across the stabilisation trials [r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score and DASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Shoulder function and upper limb disability; used in the long-term arthroscopic stabilisation trial [r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Hand-held dynamometry of external and internal rotation
outcomeMeasures.use: Strength limb symmetry index and external rotation to internal rotation ratio

outcomeMeasures.name: Shoulder-specific return-to-sport readiness scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Psychological readiness and fear of re-injury before returning to sport

imaging.indication: Before reduction in all first-time dislocations and after reduction to confirm alignment
imaging.findings: Direction of dislocation, greater tuberosity or humeral neck fracture, glenoid rim fracture, Hill–Sachs defect (best on AP in internal rotation)

imaging.indication: Subacute work-up of first-time dislocation, persistent pain or weakness, age over 40, or surgical planning
imaging.findings: Labral and capsular tears (Bankart, ALPSA, HAGL), Hill–Sachs lesion, rotator cuff tear [r11], biceps and SLAP lesions

imaging.indication: Suspected glenoid bone loss, large Hill–Sachs lesion, recurrent instability or surgical planning
imaging.findings: Quantifies glenoid and humeral head bone loss and bony Bankart fragments

imaging.indication: Older patients with persistent weakness to look for a rotator cuff tear
imaging.findings: Full-thickness or partial cuff tear and effusion

differentials.name: Posterior shoulder dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Arm held in internal rotation and unable to externally rotate, often after a seizure or electric shock; head seen posteriorly on axillary view.

differentials.name: Multidirectional instability
differentials.distinguishing: Generalised laxity, positive sulcus sign, atraumatic subluxation in several directions with minimal force.

differentials.name: Proximal humerus fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Bony deformity, crepitus and extensive bruising; confirmed on radiograph or CT, with or without dislocation.

differentials.name: Acromioclavicular joint injury
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and step deformity at the AC joint after a fall on the point of the shoulder, with preserved glenohumeral position.

differentials.name: SLAP lesion
differentials.distinguishing: Overhead pain and clicking with biceps-labrum provocation, without a frank dislocation history.

differentials.name: Traumatic rotator cuff tear
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden weakness and inability to elevate after the injury, especially in people over 40; may coexist with dislocation [r11].

differentials.name: Clavicle fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Localised bony tenderness and deformity over the clavicle after a direct fall.

differentials.name: Brachial plexus traction injury (burner)
differentials.distinguishing: Transient burning pain and arm weakness after a contact event, with a full, stable shoulder and neck-origin signs.

redFlags: Pale, cold or pulseless hand, expanding haematoma or severe distal pain: axillary artery or vascular injury (more likely in older people or after forceful or delayed reduction). Emergency vascular assessment.

Deltoid paralysis, regimental badge numbness or any new neurological deficit: axillary or brachial plexus injury. Document before and after reduction and refer if there is no recovery within the expected time (most recover within 4 months, but 8 of 101 had persistent motor loss) [r12].

Fracture on radiograph (humeral neck, displaced greater tuberosity, glenoid rim) or a dislocation that cannot be reduced: do not attempt closed reduction in the clinic. Send to the emergency department for imaging and orthopaedic opinion.

Persistent weakness or inability to elevate the arm after reduction, particularly in people over 40 years: probable rotator cuff tear. Arrange urgent ultrasound or MRI and an orthopaedic opinion [r11].

A 'dislocation' in a patient with fixed internal rotation after a seizure or electric shock, or a dislocation in a child with open growth plates: posterior dislocation or physeal fracture. Obtain an axillary view and refer urgently.

Shoulder pain with chest pressure, breathlessness or sweating, or pain not related to shoulder movement: consider cardiac or visceral referred pain rather than a shoulder cause and seek urgent medical assessment.
New fever, wound drainage, severe pain or erythema after surgical stabilisation: possible joint infection. Refer back to the surgeon the same day.

management.principles: Acute management is prompt, safe closed reduction with neurovascular assessment before and after, radiographs where fracture is possible and effective analgesia. Afterwards, choose between non-operative care and early stabilisation through shared decision-making that explains the recurrence risk for the person's age, sport and goals. Surgical stabilisation reduces recurrence in trials [r5,r6], but a pooled analysis found no significant difference in functional scores and immediate surgery may not suit everyone [r6], and in a 25-year cohort about half of those aged 12–25 years treated non-operatively had not recurred or had become stable [r4]. Early stabilisation is most clearly justified in young, high-demand contact athletes [r14,r10]. In both pathways, criteria-based rehabilitation with neuromuscular training is central [r8].

medical.name: Closed reduction (scapular manipulation, FARES or traction–countertraction)
medical.description: Prompt reduction after a pre-reduction neurovascular check, usually in the emergency department or by a trained sideline clinician. A pooled analysis of 13 studies found scapular manipulation succeeded in 97% in 1.75 minutes with a pain score of 1.47, the FARES method in 92% in 2.24 minutes with pain 1.59, and traction–countertraction in 95% in 6.05 minutes with pain 4.75 [r7].

medical.name: Analgesia and procedural sedation
medical.description: Intravenous or intra-articular analgesia or sedation to relax spasm and allow reduction, followed by oral analgesia and ice. Use according to local protocol.

medical.name: Early arthroscopic Bankart repair after a first dislocation
medical.description: In a meta-analysis of five level-1 randomised trials, recurrent instability occurred in 6.3% after stabilisation versus 46.6% with sling immobilisation (mean follow-up 59.7 months), and subsequent instability surgery in 4.0% versus 30.8% [r5]. A separate meta-analysis of 12 trials found re-dislocation in 7.5% versus 53.0% and return to play in 83.5% versus 66.0%, but no significant difference in functional scores [r6]. In a randomised trial of people under 30 years, the authors recommended immediate arthroscopic stabilisation for a subset of higher-level athletes in risky sports such as rugby, football, kayaking and rock climbing [r14]. Comparators were mostly immobilisation, not modern supervised rehabilitation. Offer to young, high-demand contact athletes, and discuss the trade-offs with everyone else.

medical.name: Delayed (off-season) stabilisation for in-season contact athletes
medical.description: In 45 intercollegiate contact athletes followed in a prospective cohort, 4 of 10 (40%) managed non-operatively with accelerated rehabilitation returned to play without recurrence the following season, compared with 26 of 29 (90%) who had surgery; surgery made it 5.8 times more likely (95% CI 1.77–18.97) to complete the subsequent season without recurrence [r10]. The cohort was small and non-randomised.

medical.name: Bone-block procedures or remplissage for significant bone loss or failed repair
medical.description: Procedures such as the Latarjet are considered by shoulder surgeons for substantial glenoid or humeral bone loss, or after failed soft-tissue repair.

medical.name: Surgical repair of a rotator cuff tear after dislocation
medical.description: In a systematic review of level III and IV studies, surgical repair improved pain relief and patient satisfaction compared with non-operative management in people with a concomitant cuff tear, and repair with capsulolabral repair helped restore stability. Consider in the appropriately active patient, particularly over 40 years [r11].

medical.name: Short-term sling for comfort
medical.description: A sling for a few days to about 3 weeks helps comfort and early protection. Immobilisation after the primary dislocation did not change the prognosis in a 25-year cohort [r4], so use it for comfort only and start gentle movement early.

medical.name: Prolonged rigid immobilisation to prevent recurrence
medical.description: Immobilisation after the primary dislocation, whether applied or not, did not change recurrence in a prospective 25-year cohort [r4]. Prolonged immobilisation risks stiffness and weakness.

medical.name: Immobilisation in external rotation
medical.description: A Cochrane review of seven trials (704 participants) found the certainty of evidence very low for all outcomes: it was uncertain whether external-rotation immobilisation changed re-dislocation compared with internal rotation (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.38–1.19), and no trial evaluated rehabilitation [r1]. Not a routine recommendation.

physio.name: Supervised neuromuscular shoulder exercise
physio.description: In a randomised trial of 56 patients with primary or recurrent traumatic anterior dislocation, 12 weeks of supervised neuromuscular exercise (seven individually progressed exercises) improved WOSI score more than a home-based standard exercise program (mean difference −228.1, 95% CI −430.5 to −25.6, against a minimal clinically important difference of 250), and 11% versus 25% went on to or were referred for surgery (not statistically significant) [r8]. Evidence is from a single small trial and longer follow-up is needed.

physio.name: Rotator cuff, scapular and kinetic chain strengthening with proprioceptive training
physio.description: Progressive strengthening of external and internal rotators and scapular stabilisers, with closed-chain rhythmic stabilisation, to build dynamic stability. Used in both non-operative and post-operative pathways.

physio.name: Education on recurrence risk, activity modification and shared decision-making
physio.description: Explain recurrence risk by age, sex and laxity [r3] and that many people do well non-operatively [r4]. Plan sport participation, season timing and when to revisit the surgical option.

physio.name: Return-to-sport shoulder bracing or harness
physio.description: A restrictive brace or harness may be used to limit the vulnerable abduction and external rotation position during early return to contact sport. Evidence for recurrence prevention is limited and it does not replace rehabilitation.

education: Most of the pain eases within a few weeks after the shoulder is put back, but the torn labrum often does not heal on its own, so rehabilitation focuses on stability and control.
The chance of the shoulder coming out again is highest in people aged 40 or under, especially active men, and it is highest in the first few years. Many people still do well without surgery [r3,r4].

Surgery lowers the chance of a repeat dislocation, but function scores were not significantly different in a pooled analysis, so it is a choice to make with your surgeon and physiotherapist based on your sport and goals [r5,r6].
Keep moving the elbow, wrist and hand. Use the sling for comfort for only a short time, and start gentle shoulder movement early.
Avoid the 'at risk' position (arm out to the side and rotated outward, with the arm pushed behind you) until your physiotherapist says it is safe.
Tell your clinician urgently about new numbness, weakness lifting the arm or a cold, pale hand.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and follows the same logic for non-operative care and after surgical stabilisation, with the post-operative pathway following the surgeon's protocol (range restrictions, usually in external rotation, for the first weeks). A randomised trial used a neuromuscular exercise program of seven exercises that progressed individually from a basic level of 2 × 20 repetitions each day to an elite level of 2 × 10 repetitions three times a week over 12 weeks [r8]. The stages below are typical, and criteria override time. Avoid combined abduction, external rotation and extension, the position of dislocation, until strength and control are restored.

stages.name: Protect and restore early movement
goals: Maintain elbow, wrist and hand function
Restore pain-free passive and assisted elevation within limits
Begin low-load activation of the cuff and scapular muscles
precautions: Avoid abduction and external rotation beyond about 30–45° and avoid extension behind the body
Use the sling for comfort only, not as long-term immobilisation [r4]
Repeat the neurovascular screen if any deficit was present, and refer if it persists

exercises.name: Pendulum (Codman) swings
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang loose and swing by moving the trunk

exercises.name: Elbow, wrist and hand range of motion and grip
Scapular setting (retraction and gentle depression)
exercises.cues: Gently draw the shoulder blades back and down; avoid shrugging

exercises.name: Submaximal isometric internal and external rotation at the side
exercises.dosage: 5 × 10 s at about 20–30% effort, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Press into the wall with the elbow bent and the arm by your side

exercises.name: Supported elevation in the scapular plane to about 90°
exercises.cues: Use the other hand to help; stay below 90° and in front of the body

progressionCriteria: Resting pain ≤ 3/10 and sleeping without regular waking
Pain-free passive elevation to about 90° and passive external rotation to about 30–45°
Active elbow and hand function and no new neurological signs

stages.name: Restore range and neuromuscular control
goals: Full or near-full pain-free range except end-range external rotation in abduction
precautions: Avoid combined abduction, external rotation and extension positions
Progress range and load only if the shoulder remains calm for 24 hours
After surgical stabilisation, follow the surgeon's range and strengthening timetable

exercises.name: Side-lying external rotation
exercises.dosage: 2–3 × 15 with a light dumbbell, daily progressing to 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Keep the elbow tucked to the ribs and rotate slowly

exercises.name: Band external and internal rotation at the side
exercises.cues: Keep the upper arm still and shoulder blade set

exercises.name: Scaption raise to 90°
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Thumb up, lift in the scapular plane

exercises.name: Band or dumbbell row
exercises.cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down

exercises.name: Wall slide and wall weight shifts (closed chain)
exercises.cues: Keep the shoulder blades moving; avoid the head dropping forward

progressionCriteria: Active elevation to near full range with no apprehension
External and internal rotation strength ≥ 70% of the other side

stages.name: Strength and dynamic stability
goals: Restore strength to near the uninjured side
Build dynamic stability in functional and overhead positions
Gradually expose the shoulder to abduction and external rotation
precautions: Introduce 90° abduction and external rotation loading gradually, only when range and strength are adequate
Do not rush end-range loaded external rotation after surgical stabilisation

exercises.name: Push-up plus progression (wall, incline, floor)
exercises.cues: Straight trunk, protract fully at the top

exercises.name: Prone Y raise
exercises.cues: Thumbs up, lift with the lower trapezius

exercises.name: Overhead press (dumbbell)
exercises.cues: Press in the scapular plane, control the lowering

exercises.name: External rotation at 90° abduction with a band
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12, progress range gradually, 2–3 times per week
exercises.cues: Start below 90° abduction and progress to 90° with a stable shoulder blade

exercises.name: Rhythmic stabilisation and perturbation (ball on wall, held position)
exercises.cues: Match the perturbation with small, fast co-contractions

progressionCriteria: External and internal rotation strength ≥ 90% of the other side
No apprehension at 90° abduction and external rotation
Controlled push-up plus with no scapular winging

stages.name: Power, sport-specific and return to sport
stages.timeframe: Months 4–6 (longer for contact sport after surgery)
goals: Develop upper-limb power and plyometric tolerance
Prepare for contact or collision with graded exposure
precautions: Introduce contact only when all return-to-sport criteria are met and with a graded plan
Consider a brace or harness for the first season in contact sport (expert opinion)

exercises.name: Medicine-ball chest pass and overhead throw
exercises.cues: Fast, controlled release; soft landing of the catch

exercises.name: Plyometric push-up or ball drops (reactive stability)
exercises.cues: Land with elbows slightly bent and shoulder blades set

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills (throwing, serving, tackling technique with pads)
exercises.dosage: Start at about 25–30% of normal volume, build over 4–6 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality first, then volume, then intensity, then contact

exercises.name: Loaded carries and overhead hold
exercises.cues: Stack wrist, elbow and shoulder; keep the ribs down

progressionCriteria: Passes strength, hop-equivalent upper-limb and function tests (see return to sport)
Confident to return, with a score on a shoulder return-to-sport readiness scale in the agreed range
Completes graded contact exposure without symptoms

criteria: Full or near-full pain-free range of motion, with external rotation matching the other side
External and internal rotation strength and abduction at about 90% or more of the other side
No apprehension or giving way at 90° abduction and external rotation, including on the relocation and anterior release tests
Good scapular and trunk control during sport-specific tasks and plyometrics
Completes progressive sport-specific and graded contact training without symptoms
Psychologically ready: confidence in the shoulder and low fear of re-injury
Time since injury or surgery: commonly not before about 3 months after non-operative care and about 6 months after stabilisation for contact sport (clinical convention)
tests: Hand-held dynamometry for external rotation, internal rotation and abduction compared with the other side
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test
Seated single-arm shot-put or medicine-ball throw
Apprehension, relocation and anterior release tests at the end of rehabilitation
WOSI and a shoulder return-to-sport readiness scale

prognosis: Recurrence is the main concern. Recurrent instability followed 39% of first-time traumatic anterior dislocations in adults, the odds were about 13 times higher in people aged 40 years or under, and the rate declined as time from the first dislocation increased [r3]. In a prospective 25-year follow-up of 255 patients aged 12–40 years managed non-operatively, 43% of shoulders had not re-dislocated, 7% re-dislocated once, 14.4% had recurrent dislocations that became stable and 7.9% remained recurrent, and 27% had surgery for instability; immobilisation did not change prognosis, and gender and athletic activity did not affect the redislocation rate [r4]. Rates in young, active populations can be higher: in a series of patients under 24 years, 90% of those treated non-operatively developed recurrent instability [r2]. After surgical stabilisation, return to play was reported in 83.5% versus 66.0% after conservative care, with no significant difference in functional scores [r6]. In intercollegiate contact athletes, 90% of those who had surgery returned to play without recurrence the following season, compared with 40% of those managed non-operatively [r10]. Nerve injuries recover partially or completely within about 4 months in most people [r12]. Long-term arthropathy after recurrent instability is a recognised concern but was not quantified in the sources reviewed.
prevention: Maintain rotator cuff, scapular and trunk strength and proprioception, particularly after a first dislocation (neuromuscular training) [r8]
Teach safe tackling and falling technique in contact sports and avoid arm-first tackles with the arm abducted and externally rotated
Complete rehabilitation and meet return-to-sport criteria before returning to contact or collision sport, rather than relying on time alone
Discuss early stabilisation with young, high-demand contact athletes after a first dislocation, given high recurrence rates [r14,r10]
A sports brace or harness may reduce exposure to the vulnerable position, but evidence for preventing recurrence is limited
clinicalPearls: Always examine and document the axillary nerve (deltoid contraction and regimental badge sensation) and distal pulses before and after reduction. Nerve injury is common in dislocation [r12].
Over 40 years, suspect a rotator cuff tear if weakness or inability to elevate persists after reduction; early imaging and referral change management [r11].
A greater tuberosity fracture is associated with a lower risk of recurrence (odds ratio 0.13) [r3], but it also means a different injury pattern, so check displacement and cuff continuity.
Use the relocation and anterior release tests rather than relying on apprehension alone [r13]. Always combine them with history and, if available, imaging.
The evidence on immobilisation position is very low certainty [r1]. Prioritise early comfortable movement and neuromuscular training over rigid positions.

In-season contact athletes face a real trade-off: playing on gives a high chance of another event, whereas off-season stabilisation gave better return-to-play without recurrence in a small cohort [r10]. Make the decision explicit and shared.

animation.title: How an anterior shoulder dislocation happens

captions.text: A rugby player runs to make a tackle with the right arm out to the side.
The arm is abducted and externally rotated, ready to wrap.
Contact drives the arm back into more external rotation and extension.
The humeral head levers forward out of the socket, and the shoulder dislocates.
The player goes down holding the arm away from the body.
Zooming into the right shoulder, viewed from the front.
In abduction and external rotation, the anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament holds the head in.
The force drives the humeral head forward against the anteroinferior capsule and labrum.
The labrum and ligament tear off the glenoid rim, the Bankart lesion.
The head slides forward and below the coracoid.
The back of the head is dented against the glenoid rim, the Hill–Sachs lesion.
Blood fills the joint, and the axillary nerve can be stretched or bruised.
Reduction puts the head back, but the labral tear remains, which is why recurrence is common.
Healthy capsulolabral and ligament collagen: crimped, aligned type I fibres.
Forced external rotation straightens the crimp and loads the fibres.
Beyond the elastic range, fibrils slide and begin to fail.
The ligament and labrum fail or peel off the glenoid.
Torn vessels bleed into the joint.
Inflammation: neutrophils and macrophages clear debris.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised collagen, and the labrum often fails to re-attach firmly.
Remodelling aligns collagen, but the scar is lax, so muscle control is the main source of stability.
